title: Universal In-Plane Confined Growth of Mesoporous Metal–Organic Framework Crystalline Heterostructures
abstract: Abstract Constructing mesoporous MOF heterostructures on conductive two-dimensional hosts remains challenging because interfacial contact and pore accessibility are rarely optimized simultaneously. Herein, we report a universal in-plane confined growth strategy for mesoporous UiO-66-NH2/MXene heterostructures featuring continuous interfacial contact and vertically accessible mesochannels. In contrast to conventional particle-on-sheet hybrids, the resulting architecture enables improved electrolyte penetration, shortened Zn2+ transport pathways, and efficient interfacial electron transfer. By regulating micellar assembly at the interface, an optimal mesostructural regime is identified in which ion accessibility and structural confinement are best balanced. Consequently, the optimized heterostructure delivers a high energy density of 163.9 Wh kg–1, excellent rate capability (∼68% retention over a 50-fold current increase), and ∼100% capacity retention over 50,000 cycles. Kinetic analyses and ex situ studies further show that the interfacial mesoporous architecture suppresses diffusion limitations and preserves structural integrity during Zn2+ storage. Moreover, the assembly concept shows transferability across substrates of different dimensionalities, highlighting its broader utility for constructing mesoporous crystalline heterostructures. This work provides an effective route to mesoporous MOF heterostructures and a generalizable design principle for hybrid crystalline electrodes.

title: Reorganization of Interfacial Water by Cu–Ru Interfaces for Efficient Nitrate-to-Ammonia Electrosynthesis
abstract: Abstract Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction offers a sustainable route for ammonia (NH3) synthesis, yet its efficiency is limited by sluggish N–O bond cleavage, incomplete NOx hydrogenation, and competing hydrogen evolution reaction. However, how catalyst structural engineering regulates the interfacial microenvironment remains unclear, despite its critical importance for constructing efficient catalysts. Here, we report a Cu3Ru7 catalyst with abundant Cu–Ru interfaces, where interface-induced water reorganization enables efficient NH3 production. The Cu3Ru7 catalyst exhibits an impressive NH3 formation rate of 19.7 mmol h–1 cm–2 at 5 A cm–2 in a membrane electrode assembly (MEA) electrolyzer and remains stable at 2 A cm–2 with an NH3 Faradaic efficiency of ∼86% for 500 h. A scale-up demonstration using a 100 cm2 MEA electrolyzer affords an NH3 formation rate up to 1.5 mol h–1 at 400 A. The in situ attenuated total reflectance surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS) reveals that Cu3Ru7 catalyst establishes a moderate interfacial hydrogen-bond network, which creates a water-mediated interfacial micro environment that facilitates NOx deoxygenation and subsequent NHx formation. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations further reveal that the Cu–Ru interface stabilizes the dissociating oxygen atom through a persistent and dynamically connected hydrogen-bond network, thereby facilitating sequential NO3– → NO2 → NO conversion. Meanwhile, the surrounding Cu matrix attenuates the excessive *H accumulation characteristic of Ru, suppressing the hydrogen evolution reaction. This work establishes Cu–Ru interface-induced interfacial water reorganization as a strategy for improving electrocatalytic nitrate reduction performance.

title: Sequential Electrochemical Construction of Hierarchical LIG/PPy/MnO2 Microsupercapacitors with High Areal Capacitance and Device-Level Stability
abstract: Abstract Achieving high areal energy storage in flexible microsupercapacitors while maintaining compatibility with direct planar patterning remains challenging, particularly when multiple pseudocapacitive components must be sequentially integrated without compromising electrode accessibility or device level performance. In this paper, we develop a sequential electrochemical construction strategy to integrate polypyrrole (PPy) and manganese dioxide (MnO2) directly onto interdigitated laser-induced graphene (LIG) electrodes without preformed composite powders, slurry casting, or polymer binders. Porous LIG serves as the conductive framework and current collector, followed by in situ PPy electropolymerization and subsequent MnO2 electrodeposition. Systematic control of LIG processing, PPy growth, MnO2 deposition, and gel electrolyte composition establishes a fabrication window that balances electrical conductivity, pseudocapacitive material loading, and structural accessibility while preserving the underlying porous LIG architecture. Stepwise LIG, LIG/PPy, and LIG/PPy/MnO2 controls exhibit the same performance hierarchy at both the individual electrode and complete device levels, demonstrating that the electrochemical gains introduced during sequential functionalization are retained after complete microsupercapacitor (MSC) assembly. The resulting LIG/PPy/MnO2 device delivers an areal capacitance of 621.2 mF cm–2 at 0.37 mA cm–2 and a maximum areal energy density of 55.22 μWh cm–2 at 0.1494 mW cm–2. Extended rate measurements further demonstrate continued electrochemical operation up to 5 mA cm–2 under substantially increased current demand. The device retains 97.04% of its flat state capacitance at 180° static bending, exhibits a device-to-device RSD of 2.29%, retains 94.5% capacitance after 60 days of ambient storage, and maintains 85.1% after 5000 GCD cycles. Series integration further extends the operating voltage from 0.8 to 2.4 V with predictable electrical scaling and enables three MSCs to power a red LED for approximately 183 s. These results establish a directly patterned and independently controlled approach for translating hierarchical pseudocapacitive construction into high areal energy storage, reproducible device performance, and scalable voltage output.

title: Coordination-directed synthesis of two-dimensional metal-organic covalent organic frameworks
abstract: Metal-organic covalent organic frameworks (MOCOFs) combine the advantages of covalent and metal-organic frameworks, but research remains sparse due to characterization difficulties, leaving unclear whether their formation is covalent- or coordination-directed. To date, only a few three-dimensional MOCOFs have been reported, while two-dimensional (2D) MOCOFs remain unexplored. Here, we strategically synthesize two single-crystal 2D MOCOFs with high porosity, denoted as PUMC-1 and PUMC-2. Leveraging three-dimensional electron diffraction, we are able to elucidate their formation process in detail. First, one-dimensional coordination polymers (1D CPs) are constructed from two sub-building units: tetrakis(4-aminophenyl) porphyrin and cobalt(II) trans-A₂B₂ porphyrin. Second, 1D CPs with covalent extension sites are used to construct two distinct 2D MOCOF conformations via covalent self-assembly under different conditions. Notably, the same 2D MOCOFs can also be directly obtained via one-pot synthesis with the same monomers, providing experimental evidence for a coordination-directed covalent assembly mechanism. This work not only expands the dimensionality of MOCOFs but also opens new avenues in reticular chemistry. Metal-organic covalent organic frameworks (MOCOFs) combine the advantages of covalent and metal-organic frameworks, but two-dimensional (2D) MOCOFs remain unexplored. Here, the authors synthesize two 2D MOCOFs with high porosity and elucidate their formation process in detail.

title: Pulsed photoelectrocatalysis enables efficient urea synthesis over Cu(salen)-COF
abstract: Abstract Electrocatalytic urea synthesis from carbon dioxide and nitrate under ambient conditions offers a sustainable alternative to the energy-intensive Bosch-Meiser process. However, its efficiency is constrained by the spatiotemporal mismatch of key carbon and nitrogen intermediates at the catalyst-electrolyte interface. Herein, we address this limitation through interfacial microenvironment optimization combining ionic liquid modification of copper-salen covalent organic framework, pulsed electrolysis, and photoelectrocatalytic coupling. The ionic liquid modification enriches carbon dioxide and facilitates interfacial charge transfer, pulsed electrolysis promotes the dynamic matching of carbon and nitrogen intermediates, and photoelectrocatalytic coupling boosts interfacial electron accumulation. The integrated system achieves a urea yield rate of 69.2 mmol g cat −1 h −1 with a Faradaic efficiency of 56.7% in an H-type cell and 82.5% in a flow cell. In this work, we establish a generalizable strategy for efficient urea electrosynthesis via hierarchical interfacial control and highlight the potential of pulsed photoelectrocatalysis.

title: Rigid Double‐Spiro‐Grid Polymer Regulates Donor Fibrillar Pre‐Assembly and Acceptor Interdiffusion in Layer‐by‐Layer Organic Solar Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT Layer‐by‐layer (LBL) fabrication of organic solar cells (OSCs) decouples donor and acceptor deposition, which, however, induces difficulties in controlling donor crystallization and acceptor interdiffusion. Here, we introduce NPSG, a fully conjugated double‐spiro‐grid polymer, to regulate donor fibrillar pre‐assembly before acceptor deposition. Morphological results reveal that NPSG shifts D18 assembly from loosely associated aggregates toward pronounced fibrillar pre‐assemblies in solution. Molecular dynamics simulations further suggest that the rigid NPSG backbone provides multiple noncovalent interaction sites that favor anisotropic association between D18 chain segments. During film formation, these fibrillar precursors evolve into a coherent and solvent‐resistant donor framework, which moderates L8‐BO interdiffusion and promotes a vertically graded, double fibrillar heterojunction. The resulting morphology facilitates interfacial charge transfer, improves the balance of electron and hole transport, and suppresses nongeminate recombination. Consequently, the optimized D18+NPSG/L8‐BO devices achieve a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 21.2%, with a certified value of 20.7%. This strategy also improves device reproducibility, processing tolerance, applicability across different donor/acceptor systems, and operational stability under maximum‐power‐point (MPP) tracking. These findings establish donor‐underlayer pre‐assembly regulation as an effective strategy for efficient and robust sequentially processed OSCs.

title: Surface‐Coordinated Gas–Solid Polymerization Enables Quasi‐2D Polyphenylacetylene Single‐Crystalline Nanoribbons
abstract: ABSTRACT Two‐dimensional (2D) conjugated polymer single crystals are highly desirable for optoelectronics, yet their realization is limited by the intrinsic coupling between molecular‐weight buildup and chain entanglement, which disrupts long‐range order. Here, we report a gas–solid interfacial polymerization strategy that decouples monomer diffusion from chain propagation, enabling the growth of quasi‐2D polyphenylacetylene (PPA) single‐crystalline nanoribbons on Cu/CuO x surfaces. This process is likely enabled by surface coordination‐assisted activation of phenylacetylene and directional π‐stacking‐driven assembly, which suppress chain entanglement and promote crystallographic ordering. As a result, micrometer‐scale PPA single‐crystalline nanoribbons with left‐handed cis‐transoidal helical chains and long‐range crystallinity are obtained. Under an ideal fully extended‐chain model, the PPA chains exhibit a geometrically estimated upper‐bound molecular weight of up to ∼3.7 × 10 9 g mol − 1 . The resulting PPA nanoribbons exhibit efficient charge transport and broadband photodetection from 375 to 1550 nm, with a responsivity of 30.1 A W − 1 and a detectivity of 8.65 × 10 1 2 Jones. This interfacial synthesis strategy provides a route to overcoming the trade‐off between molecular‐weight buildup and structural order in conjugated polymers, offering opportunities for quasi‐2D polymer semiconductors in flexible optoelectronics and programmable chiral materials.

title: Chemically Fueled Amplification of Supramolecular Asymmetry with Double Chiroptical Inversion
abstract: Abstract Amplification of asymmetry in supramolecular polymers is typically studied under equilibrium conditions in apolar solvents, while examples in aqueous media, under nonequilibrium conditions or under temporal chemical control remain scarce. Here we demonstrate chemically fueled amplification of supramolecular asymmetry in water using perylene diimide (PDI) derivatives. The chemically fueled reaction cycle uses sodium dithionite to reduce and depolymerize kinetically stable helical aggregates, while subsequent oxidation by dissolved oxygen restores them. This transient disassembly–reassembly process yields amplification of asymmetry in Majority Rules (MR) experiments that is absent in the kinetically trapped system. In Sergeants-and-Soldiers (SaS) experiments, the fueled cycle shows an unusual composition-dependent response characterized by a double chiroptical inversion as a function of sergeant fraction. A phase model captures the emergence of three composition regimes and rationalizes the observed CD response. Overall, we show how chemical fuels can regulate asymmetry amplification in aqueous supramolecular polymers and highlight the role of phase competition in complex chiral self-assembly.

title: Site Sensitivity Resulting in Selective Hydroxylamine Electrosynthesis
abstract: Abstract The electroreduction of nitrogen oxides offers a promising route for green synthesis of hydroxylamine (NH2OH). Although Pd exhibited high selectivity toward NH2OH production experimentally, we found the dominant hollow sites of pristine Pd prefer ammonia production via the NOH*-pathway. This discrepancy was resolved by unveiling the critical roles of in situ hydriding of Pd under operando conditions. Using Grand Canonical Monte Carlo simulations driven by machine learning potential, we demonstrated the potential-dependent structural evolution from pristine Pd to palladium hydride (PdHx) under −0.11 to −0.51 V vs RHE. For the in situ-generated PdHx surfaces with some amorphous or disordering features, the dominant hollow sites of Pd are blocked by adsorbed H* species, thereby repelling NO* to adsorb obliquely on PdHx top sites. The adsorption configuration of NO* steers the reaction pathway from NOH* to HNO* formation, leading to NH2OH* production eventually. In addition, the PdHx top sites exhibit generally downshifted d-band centers, promoting NH2OH* desorption and preventing its over-reduction to ammonia. At last, a site sensitivity was proposed for hydroxylamine electrosynthesis based on the analysis on a variety of catalysts; the formation energies of HNO* vs NOH* and the adsorption energy of NH2OH* were identified as important features resulting in high hydroxylamine selectivity.

title: Solvent-Directed Supramolecular Reconstruction Through Coupled Coordination-Bond Dynamics and Covalent-Bond Formation
abstract: Abstract Understanding how external stimuli actively direct bond reorganization and supramolecular reconstruction remains a fundamental challenge in adaptive self-assembly. Although solvent-induced transformations are widely observed in supramolecular systems, the molecular mechanisms by which solvents simultaneously regulate coordination-bond dynamics and covalent-bond formation remain poorly understood. Herein, we report a rare cluster-based triply interlocked [2]catenane, [(Tp*WS3Cu3)8(L)12(OTf)8](OTf)8 ([1(OTf)8], Tp* = tris(3,5-dimethylpyrazolyl)borate; L = (Z)-4,4′-(but-1-en-3-yne-1,4-diyl)dipyridine; OTf– = trifluoromethanesulfonate), which undergoes methanol-directed supramolecular reconstruction into an octahedral cage. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction establishes the structures of both the interlocked precursor and the reconstructed product, while solution-state NMR spectroscopy and control experiments reveal a rapid and highly selective reconstruction process. Density functional theory calculations propose key intermediates and elucidate the dual mechanistic role of methanol during the reconstruction. Methanol promotes displacement of weakly coordinated triflate ligands and perturbs the local coordination environment, thereby initiating coordination-bond reorganization. Subsequent methanol coordination further recognizes the coordination framework and facilitates alkyne-sulfide addition that stabilizes the emerging octahedral architecture. The reconstruction therefore proceeds through coupled coordination-bond dynamics and covalent-bond formation rather than simple cage dissociation and reassembly. These findings provide a molecular-level mechanistic framework for understanding how solvent molecules can actively direct supramolecular reconstruction through the interplay of coordination chemistry and chemical reactivity.

title: In Situ Probing of Small‐Molecule Electrolysis Using Ambient‐Pressure X‐Ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy
abstract: ABSTRACT Electrocatalytic small‐molecule conversion addresses the need to couple renewable electricity with sustainable fuel and chemical production, yet challenges remain in resolving the dynamic gas/solid/liquid interfaces that govern catalytic activity, selectivity and stability. A key challenge is to correlate catalyst structures, reaction intermediates and local interfacial environments under comparable operating conditions. Ambient‐pressure x‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy (APXPS) provides surface‐sensitive and chemically specific information on catalyst chemical states, interfacial species and local electrostatic environments at the same working interface, enabling direct correlations between catalyst evolution and reaction intermediates. We offer a forward‐looking review of APXPS for probing gas/solid/liquid interfaces in small‐molecule electrolysis. We discuss three categories of electrochemical XPS/APXPS configurations: quasi‐in situ XPS, in which electrochemically treated catalysts are transferred under protected conditions for post‐reaction analysis; thin‐electrolyte‐film (dip‐and‐pull) APXPS, which probes a potential‐controlled interface through a nanometer‐scale liquid film; and membrane‐based APXPS, which accesses catalyst–ionomer–electrolyte interfaces. We introduce present‐day challenges in electrochemical APXPS and describe a vision towards more realistic operating conditions, higher time resolution and multimodal measurements integrated with theoretical and data‐driven spectral analysis. These developments provide potential avenues to establish reliable structure–intermediate–environment relationships in the further development of small‐molecule electrocatalysis.

title: Porous Framework Assembly Creates Functional Tertiary Folds in Small Peptides
abstract: Abstract There is significant interest in recreating the protein tertiary structure in simpler systems, which can enable the precise and modular organization of multiple functional groups for enhancing molecular recognition and catalysis. Small peptides are minimalist analogs of proteins; however, their limited size highly disfavors folding into tertiary structures, especially those that also possess open binding sites needed for function. Here, we report that 3-dimensional self-assembly into a porous crystalline framework overcomes this limitation, producing modular tertiary structures in peptides shorter than 20 amino acids with tunable binding sites. As shown by X-ray crystallography, this framework-mediated folding tolerates many sequences with a broad range of functional groups, and it generates precise confined environments that are dynamic and mutationally robust. Thus, these pores can be programmed to selectively bind complex molecular guests such as nucleotides and perfluoroalkyl substances through the cooperative engagement of up to 10 distinct residues. These results demonstrate that a well-defined tertiary structure can exist in very short peptides and can impart tunable protein-like function to synthetic porous materials.

title: Programmable Directional Assembly of Hydrogen-Bonded Lead Organic Chalcogenolates
abstract: Abstract Controlling the directional assembly of metal organic chalcogenolates (MOCs) with atomic precision remains a synthetic challenge yet represents a critical step toward advancing their programmable syntheses and property investigations. Herein, we present a “hydrogen-bond-directed assembly” strategy to drive the formation of single-crystalline, hydrogen-bonded lead organic chalcogenolates (H-LOCs), offering an ideal platform for elucidating their structure–property relationships. By strategically functionalizing thiophenol with regiochemically or electronically distinct substituents, we achieved precise control at the ligand–ligand interface, yielding six distinct H-LOC architectures mediated by interlayer, intralayer, or cooperative hybrid hydrogen-bonding interactions. These programmed hydrogen-bonding interactions play an essential role in crystal growth, enabling the formation of large single crystals of two-dimensional (2D) LOCs. Combined structural and optical characterizations reveal a linear correlation between the ligand electronic effects and optical bandgaps of the materials, culminating in a narrow bandgap of 1.55 eV for the most electron-donating substituent. Most importantly, the reversible nature of these interfacial hydrogen bonds endows the H-LOCs with excellent solution-processability, allowing them to be fabricated into highly stable films with ambient durability exceeding two months─thereby unlocking their potential for optoelectronic devices.

title: Geometry-Programmed Connectivity Enables Predictive Assembly of Diamond-Family Colloidal Crystals
abstract: Abstract The predictive assembly of open colloidal crystals requires encoding specific connectivity rules into building blocks that are otherwise isotropic and lack inherent directionality. Here we introduce a geometry-programmed connectivity strategy in which spatial confinement, rather than surface patterning or lattice templating, programs not only particle coordination but also the accessible bonding arrangement that governs network connectivity. We implement this concept using tetrahedral DNA origami frameworks that confine DNA-functionalized spherical particles and restrict their accessible bonding pathways to four tetrahedrally arranged patches, thereby converting isotropic colloids into effective tetravalent building blocks with geometrically prescribed connectivity. A geometric hard-contact model translates these confinement-defined connectivity rules and the linker-defined interaction range into coordination regimes and lattice symmetry, yielding a predictive phase diagram. Guided by this model, we experimentally realize diamond-family colloidal crystals featuring the coexistence of cubic diamond and double diamond phases, as well as zinc blende and double zinc blende phases. Photonic band-structure calculations predict that the experimentally realized cubic diamond and zinc blende topologies can support complete PBGs in the deep-ultraviolet regime. We thus establish a predictive form of colloidal topological engineering, in which confinement geometry programs local connectivity and selects emergent crystal topology.

title: Thermoresponsive Miktoarm Glycopolymer–Protein Conjugates Based on Molecular Recognition: Synthesis and Self-Assembly
abstract: Abstract Simultaneously modifying proteins with different polymers can enrich protein functions and provide various polymer–protein conjugates. Investigating the self-assembly of complex amphiphilic polymer–protein conjugates offers insights into the formation of different protein structures. Herein, we synthesize a new bifunctional chain transfer agent with both an adamantyl group and a biotin group (AB-CTA) to prepare the thermoresponsive poly(di(ethylene glycol) methyl ether methacrylate) with the two functional groups (AB-PDEGMA). Two types of glycopolymers were synthesized and each was modified with a β-cyclodextrin (β-CD) group. AB-PDEGMA was mixed with the β-CD-modified glycopolymer, affording a block copolymer. It was then conjugated to streptavidin (SA) to prepare miktoarm glycopolymer–protein conjugates. The whole process is modularized based on molecular recognition of adamantane/β-CD and SA/biotin. It is accessible to adjust the polymer type and chain length to prepare the desired conjugates. Self-assembly of the miktoarm glycopolymer-SA conjugates was investigated above their lower critical solution temperatures. Assemblies including spherical micelles, compound micelles with patchy structures, and proteinosomes could be obtained. The influences of the binding number of the block copolymer and PDEGMA chain length on self-assembly were revealed, which was consistent with conclusions reported in previous simulation articles.

title: From Accurate Quantum Chemistry to Converged Thermodynamics for Ion Pairing in Solution
abstract: Abstract Quantitative prediction of thermodynamic properties in solution is essential for translating atomistic simulations into reliable chemical insight. As an exemplar system, the behavior of CaCO3 in water has been widely studied to understand its mineralization in seawater, with potential implications for carbon-capture strategies. However, making accurate computational predictions has been a long-standing challenge, requiring both highly accurate electronic structure methods and extensive statistical sampling. Here, we combine advances in machine learning and electronic structure theory to fully resolve the ion pairing free energy of CaCO3 with explicit solvation. We show that achieving quantitative agreement with experiment requires going beyond density functional theory up to the “gold-standard” coupled cluster theory with single, double, and perturbative triple excitations [CCSD(T)]. We generate a set of systematically improvable models, enabling reliable insights into the initial association mechanism of Ca and CO3 ions prior to nucleation while fully quantifying enthalpic and entropic effects. These quantitatively accurate models further resolve a long-standing lack of consensus surrounding the hydration mechanism of the calcium ion in solution. Our results demonstrate that CCSD(T)-level thermodynamic predictions of complex aqueous systems can now be routinely achieved.

title: Electronic Polarization Induced Coordination Directs Crystal Facet Engineering for Cryogenic Rechargeable Li||Cl 2 Batteries
abstract: ABSTRACT Controlling the crystallographic facet orientation of in situ deposited products in conversion‐type batteries remains a fundamental challenge, as conventional synthesis‐based strategies cannot be applied to phases that nucleate and grow electrochemically during cell operation. Here, taking rechargeable Li||Cl 2 batteries as a model system, we elucidate the complete AlCl 4 − ‐mediated catalytic cycle governing the LiCl‐to‐Cl 2 charging conversion and identify the intrinsic covalent rigidity of the Al─Cl bond as the rate‐determining factor. On this basis, we propose an electronic polarization induced coordination (EPIC) strategy in which an in situ‐assembled [AlCl 2 (BZA) 2 ] + coordination cation (BZA = benzamide) activates directional N─H···Cl hydrogen bonds that selectively weaken the Al─Cl bond and lower the catalytic energy barrier. This molecular‐level intervention simultaneously redirects LiCl crystal growth from passivating {100} cubes toward dispersed {111}‐faceted nanocrystals through adsorption‐induced surface‐energy inversion, and operando x‐ray diffraction identifies these nanocrystals as the preferentially cycled, highly reversible phase, establishing a complete causal chain from coordination chemistry through catalytic kinetics to crystal facet engineering via a single design element. Li||Cl 2 cells employing the EPIC electrolyte sustain over 2500 stable cycles at −40°C under 1 A g −1 , tolerate current densities up to 30 A g −1 , and deliver 6.06 Ah in a cylindrical cell (ER26500) at 25°C.

title: Engineering High‐Performance Flexible Electronics Through Scalable Manufacturing: Interplay of Materials, Processing, and Morphology
abstract: ABSTRACT Flexible electronics have garnered extensive attention in recent years considering their promising applications across diverse fields such as communications, energy, display, healthcare, and wearable devices. Unlike laboratory‐scale fabrication and integration, the transition of flexible electronics toward commercial applications demands scalable manufacturing that ensures high performance, large‐area reproducibility, high yield, and throughput. However, achieving scalable manufacturing while maintaining device performance remains challenging, as fabrication scale‐up often induces variations in material assembly, morphology evolution, and device integration, which may compromise functional reliability achieved at the laboratory scale. Generally, current flexible electronic devices can be divided into two categories: planar‐type and fiber‐type devices, representing two complementary platforms for realizing large‐scale and highly integrated systems. In this review, scalable fabrication strategies tailored for each category and the latest advances are systematically summarized. In particular, the interplay among material design, scalable processing, morphology evolution, and device integration is highlighted, with emphasis on strategies that preserve device performance during manufacturing scale‐up. Representative planar‐type and fiber‐type flexible electronic systems are further discussed to demonstrate how the synergistic optimization of material design and scalable manufacturing approaches enables high‐performance devices for diverse applications. Finally, we outline remaining challenges and future directions to inform future developments in scalable flexible electronics.

title: Cross‐Scale Decoupling of Mechanics and Kinematics in Chiral Tensegrity Metamaterials
abstract: ABSTRACT Compression‐torsion metamaterials (CTMs) that break spatial inversion symmetry face persistent trade‐offs among large deformation capacity, intrinsic stiffness, and fatigue durability. Crucially, boundary rotation induced by axial compression complicates integration with rotationally constrained engineering interfaces. Here we introduce a chiral three‐rod tensegrity cell (CTTC) paradigm that addresses these conflicts through a cross‐scale dual‐decoupling strategy. First, mechanical decoupling at the unit‐cell scale separates macroscopic shape‐morphing from large local material strain: a heterogeneous rigid‐flexible architecture channels global compression into kinematic rod displacement and uniform elastic‐network stretching, achieving 97° torsion at Level 0 and only 4.87% peak‐force degradation over 10 000 cycles at Level 3. An integrated geometric interlocking reconfigurator further enables post‐fabrication programmability of stiffness and strain‐normalized twist ratio ( R T‐S ). Second, kinematic decoupling at the assembly scale localizes torsional deformation as a boundary‐decoupled internal rotational mode, while maintaining external interfaces in pure translation. This cross‐scale framework establishes a deployable paradigm bridging metamaterial physics and robotic systems operating in geometrically constrained environments.

title: Buried CdSe Sacrificial Layer Driving Phase Evolution and Crystallization Kinetics Enables 14.78%‐Efficient DMF‐Based Kesterite Solar Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT During selenization, the inherent transport lag of Se from the film surface to the buried Mo/precursor interface causes early‐stage Se deficiency in the bottom region, creating a depth‐dependent crystallization lag that limits the homogeneity of Cu 2 ZnSn(S,Se) 4 (CZTSSe) absorbers. Here, we evaporate an ultrathin CdSe sacrificial layer at the Mo/precursor interface of N,N ‐dimethylformamide (DMF)‐derived CZTSSe absorbers. This layer is rapidly consumed at the onset of selenization, providing an in‐situ Se supply at the buried interface and effectively bypassing the intrinsic transport delay from the surface. The locally supplied Se initiates early‐stage bottom selenization and promotes the conversion of Cu 2 SnSe 3 ‐related intermediates toward CZTSSe while suppressing their persistent accumulation, enabling rear‐side nucleation and grain growth to commence substantially earlier than in the conventional surface‐dominated process. Meanwhile, the redistributed Cd 2+ partially substitutes Zn 2+ sites, reducing defect‐assisted recombination and enhancing carrier transport and extraction. The optimized device achieves a champion efficiency of 14.78% with a certified efficiency of 14.30%, establishing a new benchmark for DMF‐derived kesterite solar cells. This work demonstrates that prepositioning a sacrificial Se‐containing component at the buried interface to enable in situ release of Se offers a viable pathway for coordinating phase evolution and improving multinary chalcogenide absorber quality.

title: Interface‐Directed Two‐Dimensional Growth of Non‐Layered NiO on MoS 2 Under Coupled External Fields
abstract: ABSTRACT The controlled growth of two‐dimensional (2D) non‐layered transition metal oxides remains a key challenge in low‐dimensional material synthesis. Achieving atomically precise construction of 2D structures requires a fundamental understanding of how external fields and interfacial interactions govern nucleation and growth processes. In this work, amorphous NiO x (a‐NiO x ) was deposited onto monolayer MoS 2 , and its transformation into crystalline 2D NiO nanosheets was directly visualized in situ using environmental transmission electron microscopy. The electron beam induces the decomposition of a‐NiO x into mobile NiO x species, which migrate and nucleate on MoS 2 , demonstrating the synergistic roles of the electron beam and thermal field in NiO cluster formation and interface‐dominated epitaxial growth. Combined notch‐filtered imaging and theoretical calculations reveal that Ni–O units preferentially attach at the NiO/MoS 2 interface to form one‐dimensional growth fronts, while oriented attachment proceeds via nanosheet rotation, interfacial fusion, and defect‐mediated reconstruction, culminating in lattice relaxation into a single‐crystalline structure. High‐throughput selected‐area electron diffraction further uncovers the modulation of external fields on the multi‐path structural evolution of NiO x . This work establishes an in situ strategy to resolve nucleation and growth pathways of 2D heterostructures, enabling active control over the 2D growth of non‐layered metal oxides and advancing deterministic atomic‐level construction.

title: Smart Luminescent Materials: From Basic Luminophores to Stimuli‐Responsive Luminescent Systems
abstract: ABSTRACT Smart luminescent materials (SLMs) represent an emerging class of intelligent optical systems that can convert external stimuli into adaptive and programmable photonic outputs. By integrating molecular photophysics with dynamic structural regulation, SLMs enable precise modulation of emission intensity, wavelength, polarization, lifetime, and energy conversion pathways with high spatiotemporal controllability. Recent advances in molecular engineering, supramolecular assembly, and hierarchical material design have driven a transition from conventional luminescence switching toward multifunctional systems featuring multilevel, multistimulus, and information‐enriched optical responses. This review provides a comprehensive and mechanism‐oriented overview of recent progress in SLMs across diverse material platforms, including solution‐phase systems, solid‐state materials, dynamic hydrogels, chiral circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) systems, and lanthanide‐doped upconversion nanoparticles. Particular emphasis is placed on how external stimuli regulate excited‐state electronic structures, molecular conformations, supramolecular organizations, and hierarchical architectures to achieve adaptive luminescent behaviors. In addition, emerging strategies for stimuli‐responsive CPL regulation and intelligent photon conversion based on upconversion nanomaterials are highlighted, demonstrating how molecular‐level control can be translated into dynamic optical functionalities. Finally, current challenges and future opportunities are discussed toward the rational design of next‐generation smart luminescent materials for applications in information security, wearable electronics, soft robotics, biophotonics, and intelligent photonic devices.

title: Adaptive Discovery of Uncharted Zeolitic Imidazolate Frameworks
abstract: Abstract Discovering new zeolitic imidazolate framework (ZIF) structures remains a major challenge because their assembly depends on the nature of the linker and synthesis conditions. Here, we introduce linker width as a design parameter for ZIF synthesis. We designed 4-substituted benzimidazole linkers with expanded width and combined them with smaller linkers in an adaptive machine-learning (ML) high-throughput strategy. This adaptive discovery scheme yielded nine new mixed-linker ZIFs, including six adopting the previously unrealized bcv topology. Single-crystal structural analysis reveals ordered linker distributions in which the wider 4-substituted benzimidazolate linkers code for the formation of 10-membered-ring needed for the apertures of the bcv cage. Comparison with representative mixed-linker ZIFs further identifies the width of linkers and the extension ratio as steric descriptors of topology selection. These results provide chemically interpretable design principles for mixed-linker ZIF assembly and demonstrate how linker design coupled with ML-guided synthesis can access unexplored regions of chemical space.

title: Guest Transition Metals in Host Keplerate Nanocapsules as Supramolecular Inorganic Functional Mimics of Monooxygenase Enzymes
abstract: ABSTRACT Advanced design of supramolecules can mimic enzyme complexes. Methane monooxygenases have several subparts, hydroxylases active for alkane oxidation, and complexes and channels that regulate electron, proton, substrate, and product access to the active site. The replication of a hydroxylase active site with inclusion of regulatory functionalities within a porous Keplerate nanocapsule host was undertaken. A Cu active site guest within a Keplerate cavity was prepared by an assembly reaction using a histidine surrogate as binding site for Cu II . The guest–host assembly enables transfer of protons and electrons and enables substrate and product diffusion to and from an active site into confined space. Characterization of the guest–host complex was by NMR, XPS, infrared, and Raman spectroscopies. Cyclic voltammetry was used to identify possible hydroxylase reactivity, followed by controlled potential electrolysis to verify hydrocarbon oxygenation. Substrate scope, optimal cathodic potential, and the number of metal sites needed were surveyed. Comparison of substrate reactivity revealed that their access to the active site was rate determining. Kinetics of a “dummy” substrate and product diffusion was measured by Guest Exchange Saturation Transfer 19 F NMR. These guest–host Keplerate nanocapsules represent an initial foray into the mimicking of a complicated metalloenzyme complex in an inorganic synthetic system.

title: Hierarchical Engineering of Atomically Precise Gold Nanoclusters from Alloying to Cluster-Assembled Frameworks
abstract: Abstract Atomically precise gold nanoclusters (Au NCs) provide molecular-level platforms for understanding how atomic structure influences catalytic, photophysical, chiral, and electronic properties. Although alloying, ligand/interface engineering, and nanocluster assembly have each emerged as powerful approaches for tailoring Au NC function, they are often considered as separate design strategies. In this perspective, we organize recent advances in Au NC design across three interconnected levels of structural control: core alloying, ligand/interface engineering, and cluster-assembled materials. We discuss how alloying modifies the intrinsic electronic structure of the NC core, how ligand and interface engineering regulate the expression of these properties through electronic and structural control, and how coordination-mediated assembly organizes individual NCs into aggregates, superstructures, and crystalline frameworks with collective photophysical and electronic properties. By connecting these design strategies, this perspective provides a hierarchical view of Au NC design that links molecular precision to materials-level functionality and highlights opportunities for catalysis, sensing, optoelectronics, and nanoelectronics.

title: Operando Quantifying Li Plating Processes in Lithium‐Ion Pouch Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT Lithium‐ion batteries require high reliability and extended lifespan for practical grid storage applications, yet Li plating remains a critical hazard inducing rapid capacity fade and safety risks. The transient and heterogeneous nature of Li plating poses a significant challenge to real‐time quantitative detection. Herein, we define a critical Li‐plating areal capacity (q Li ) derived from dynamic electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (DEIS) and establish an operando strategy to accurately quantify Li plating under diverse charging conditions. Validated by operando solid‐state nuclear magnetic resonance (ssNMR)‐DEIS combined measurements, incremental capacity analysis, and mass spectrometry titration (MST), this method demonstrates high reliability, exceptional accuracy (R 2 > 0.97), and general validity across different temperatures (0°C–45°C) and battery capacities (4 to 110 mAh). A transmission line model (TLM) elucidates the physical origin of q Li : it corresponds to the critical surface coverage (∼10%, model‐derived) of lithium nuclei on graphite, marking the transition from nucleation‐dominated to growth‐controlled deposition. We further demonstrate that regulating temperature can switch the nucleation mode, thereby significantly altering q Li and the resulting plating characteristics. This study establishes a robust operando quantification platform, enabling early battery warning and adaptive fast charging to suppress excessive Li plating and extend service life in practical cells.

title: π‐Electronic Effects Dictate Interlayer Charge Transfer in Covalent Organic Frameworks With Boosted Photocatalytic Activity
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding interlayer charge transfer is central to the rational design of two‐dimensional (2D) covalent organic frameworks (COFs) for high‐performance photocatalysis. Herein, we successfully modulate the interlayer charge transfer in donor–imine–donor type COFs by regulating the π‐electronic character of knots and linkers. We demonstrate that the rigid pyrene‐based knot with profound π‐electronic effect promotes efficient interlayer charge transfer, whereas the twisted biphenyl‐based counterpart effectively inhibits it combining with experimental and theoretical calculations. Specifically, the pyrene‐based units endow enhanced conjugation, improved planarity, and strengthened π–π stacking, giving rise to a substantially larger interlayer charge transfer amount for the fully rigid R–R–COF compared with the twisted T–T–COF. Consequently, R–R–COF achieves a superior H 2 evolution rate of 80.6 mmol g −1 h −1 , 89.6 times that of T–T–COF (0.9 mmol g −1 h −1 ) under identical conditions. Additionally, we reveal that topological selectivity correlates closely with the electronic nature of the knot. This work establishes π‐electronic effect as a key determinant of both interlayer charge transfer efficiency and photocatalytic activity, and provides a rational design strategy for advanced COF‐based photocatalysts.

title: Stable and selective C( sp 3)–H halogenation over COF-modified β -Fe2O3 photoanodes
abstract: Abstract Photoelectrocatalytic synthesis provides a sustainable route to high-value organic chemicals, yet achieving high selectivity while maintaining long-term stability remains challenging because of limited interfacial reactant availability and competing radical-mediated reaction pathways. Here, we develop a COF-modified photoanode by integrating a functionalized covalent organic framework (COF) onto β-Fe2O3 to regulate aqueous C(sp3)–H halogenation. Using cyclohexane chlorination as a model reaction, the COF-modified β-Fe2O3 photoanode achieves a monochlorination selectivity of up to 96.8% under AM 1.5 G illumination (100 mW cm−2), far exceeding the 53.9% obtained over bare β-Fe2O3. Under one-sun illumination, the photoanode delivers a photocurrent density of 2.8 mA cm−2 and remains stable for 300 h, retaining approximately 95% chlorocyclohexane selectivity at the end of the test. Even under 13-sun illumination, the photocurrent density reaches approximately 35 mA cm−2, with a chlorocyclohexane selectivity of 91.9% after 100 h. The COF-modified photoanode also shows enhanced monobromination and monoiodination selectivities, demonstrating the generality of this approach.

title: Defect engineering in metal-organic frameworks for enhanced hydrogen storage: Unlocking hidden active sites – A review
abstract: While hydrogen is a promising clean energy carrier to achieve carbon neutrality, its widespread adoption has been hindered by the absence of efficient, safe, and scalable hydrogen storage solutions. Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have emerged as a new class of materials with tunable pore structures, high surface areas, and versatility in structure that recently have been explored for hydrogen storage. The performance of pristine MOFs is, however, limited by weak hydrogen–framework interactions and lack of active adsorption sites. To solve such problems, defect engineering has emerged as a promising approach by building engineered defects such as open metal sites, hierarchical porosity, hidden active centers, and enhanced transport pathways. This review discusses defect engineering strategies to improve hydrogen storage in MOFs, including hydrogen adsorption mechanisms, synthesis methods, defect chemistry, active-site generation, and defect-induced transport occurrences. The importance of integrating experimental characterization and computational modelling for understanding defect behaviour is emphasized. Recent advances in materials informatics, machine learning, and AI-assisted discovery of defect-engineered MOFs are also discussed. Lastly, the main difficulties in defect control, stability, scaling up, and predictive design are presented, along with future prospects for the development of next-generation MOFs for sustainable hydrogen-energy applications.

title: Chiral Metal–Organic Frameworks with Multiple and Highly Anisotropic Nonlinear Optical Effects
abstract: Abstract The design and construction of photonic materials with multiple and anisotropic nonlinear optical (NLO) behaviors for all-photonic device applications is an attractive but challenging task. Herein, we present a generalizable polarity–chirality synergy strategy that employs donor−π–acceptor (D-π-A)-type organic molecules as polar linkers for assembling chiral metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), in which polarity governs the NLO properties while chirality enables symmetry breaking. Through a chiral induction method, a pair of novel chiral MOFs, LaTCA-L and LaTCA-D, were synthesized by using 4,4″,4‴-tricarboxyltriphenylamine (H3TCA) as the ligand and lanthanum ions as the metal nodes. The LaTCA-L and LaTCA-D crystals simultaneously exhibit significant photoluminescence and second-order and third-order NLO effects with a second-harmonic generation (SHG) intensity of up to 11 times that of the classic KH2PO4 (KDP) crystal. In addition, the LaTCA-L crystal shows obvious linear polarization-dependent SHG, third-harmonic generation (THG), and two-photon-excited photoluminescence (2PEL) with a high degree of polarization (DOP) up to 99.0% under excitation wavelengths ranging from 900 to 1800 nm. In particular, the MOF LaTCA-L exhibits gSHG-CD values of 0.79 and 0.86 at 1030 nm, with identical circular-polarization-dependent SHG trends confirmed at 1064 and 1310 nm. Moreover, this construction strategy can be easily expanded to other D-π-A type organic ligands such as 1,3,5-tris(4-carboxyphenyl)benzene acid (H3BTB), thus opening a pathway toward designing multifunctional chiral MOFs with promising potential for photonic applications.

title: Self-Assembly Driven Modulation of Photocatalytic H2O2 Activity in Acridine-Based Derivatives
abstract: Abstract Self-assembly provides a powerful strategy for regulating the photophysical and photocatalytic properties of π-conjugated organic molecules through controlled intermolecular organization. Herein, we demonstrate that molecular aggregation can either suppress or activate photocatalysis, depending on the structural and solubility properties of the catalyst. Two organic photocatalysts, Acr-1 and Acr-2, with distinct affinities toward water, exhibit markedly different H2O2 generation behavior upon self-assembly. Hydrophilic Acr-1 efficiently produces H2O2 in aqueous 3-(N-morpholino)propanesulfonic acid (MOPS) solution in its monomeric state, whereas self-assembly suppresses its photocatalytic activity. In striking contrast, Acr-2, which is inactive in its monomeric state, becomes photocatalytically active upon self-assembly. Spectroscopic investigations indicate that aggregation in Acr-2 suppresses nonradiative deactivation pathways and promotes productive photochemical processes, thereby enabling H2O2 generation. The resulting supramolecular assemblies remain stable under continuous irradiation for up to 4 h while retaining their photocatalytic activity. Scavenger experiments combined with spectroscopic analyses further elucidate the involvement of reactive intermediates in H2O2 generation. These findings establish aggregation state as an important molecular parameter for regulating photocatalytic function and demonstrate that supramolecular self-assembly can be harnessed to switch and maintain solar-driven H2O2 generation in organic photocatalyst.

title: Massively parallel self-assembly of suspendable microcompartments for functional cell screening
abstract: Modern biology increasingly demands platforms that can compartmentalize and analyze single cells and cell-cell interactions at massive scale, yet existing compartmentalization strategies based on microfluidics suffer from critical limitations. Emerging lab-on-a-particle technologies such as nanovials enable anchored single cells or small groups of cells to be isolated and assayed in a fully suspendable and parallelized manner using standard instrumentation, although their open architectures can result in loss of growing or un-attached cells. Here, we introduce capped nanovials: self-assembling hydrogel compartments formed by docking spherical capping particles into bowl-shaped nanovials. We routinely achieve capping of >80% of all nanovials in a sample and >90% sorting yield by flow cytometry, making the capped nanovial system well-suited for preparing and running large-scale assays. Furthermore, we demonstrate stable clonal expansion of single mammalian, yeast, and bacterial cells; growth-based selections of >10,000 colonies; enhanced signal-to-noise in secretion assays; and high-purity selection of antibody-secreting cells based on activation of co-encapsulated T cell reporters (>30-fold signal, up to 100% selection purity). By combining the simplicity of a well plate with the functional precision of droplet microfluidics without requiring oil or custom instrumentation, capped nanovials realize accessible, high-throughput, and high-resolution experimentation.

title: Amyloid‐Guided Assembly of Magnetically Recyclable Enzymatic Nanofibers Toward Sustainable Biocatalysis
abstract: ABSTRACT The rational construction of recyclable protein‐based catalytic materials requires connecting molecular enzyme design with higher‐order supramolecular organization and functional recovery interfaces. This study establishes a hierarchical design strategy that integrates fusion‐enzyme engineering, amyloid‐guided self‐assembly, and magnetic immobilization. The primary amine oxidase DPAO4 and the flavin‐containing amine oxidase DMAO7 were joined through flexible or rigid linkers, and the rigid (EAAAK) 3 variant provided broad substrate coverage, greater tolerance to process‐relevant stresses, and lower interdomain fluctuations in molecular dynamics simulations. N‐terminal Sup35 1‐61 or Ure2 1‐80 domains promoted the formation of ThT‐responsive fibrillar assembly, and the resulting enzymatic nanofibers were coupled to amino‐functionalized Fe 3 O 4 @SiO 2 ‐NH 2 nanoparticles. The composites enabled magnetic separation within 30 s, catalyzed the degradation of eight biogenic amines under acidic, thermal, saline, and ethanol‐containing conditions, and retained an average of 53.2% of their initial activity after four recovery cycles. As proof‐of‐concept evaluation in complex matrices, selected systems removed up to 70.6% of total biogenic amines from fermented beverages and 69.7% from soy sauce. The distinct responses of the Sup35‐ and Ure2‐based composites suggest an association between assembly‐domain identity and catalytic performance in complex matrices. This work demonstrates a hierarchical design approach for recyclable protein‐based catalytic materials and sustainable biocatalysis.

title: Accessing Core-Functionalized DNA–Polymer Nanostructures via RAFT Polymerization-Induced Self-Assembly
abstract: Abstract DNA–polymer nanostructures with precise sequences and programmable recognition capabilities are capable of achieving spatially accurate organization of functional moieties for applications in targeted drug delivery, biosensing, bioimaging, and regenerative medicine. However, traditional synthetic routes for DNA–polymer nanostructures are cumbersome and inefficient, while existing RAFT-PISA systems are restricted to limited monomer types, leading to insufficient core functionality and poor property adjustability. Herein, we present the fabrication of core-functionalized DNA–polymer nanostructures via RAFT-PISA of a thymine-containing monomer in both DMF/water mixed solvent and pure water. Efficient and well-controlled polymerization is achieved by using a DNA-modified chain transfer agent (CTA); however, dense surface DNA chains inhibit structural evolution to form only spherical aggregates. Tuning the surface DNA density and adopting hydrophilic macromolecular CTA enable successful access to spheres, worms, and vesicles by simply regulating core chain lengths. The newly developed core-functionalized DNA–polymer nanostructures retain excellent DNA recognition capability in the shell layer. Meanwhile, they allow programmable post-polymerization morphology modulation through multiple hydrogen bonds in the core layer. This strategy not only provides a reliable approach to constructing distinct DNA–polymer nanostructures but also expands and advances PISA toward tunable core-functionalized nano-objects.

title: Magnetic Ordering Controlled by Ionic Proximity in Self-Assembled Ionic Liquid Nanostructures
abstract: Abstract Magnetic ionic liquids (MILs) commonly exhibit paramagnetic behavior because the spatially isolated and disordered arrangement of magnetic centers limits cooperative magnetic interactions. Herein, the terphenyl-based MIL 3ph-imi[FeCl4] was processed under different conditions to obtain three samples with distinct structural organizations. Liquid-nitrogen quenching produced an amorphous solid. Aging a 1.0 mg mL–1 aqueous solution at 25 °C yielded 50–90 nm spindle-shaped assemblies (Assembly-1) containing locally ordered domains, whereas aging at 5 °C generated ca. 40 μm platelets (Assembly-2) with lamellar periodicity and extended in-plane crystalline order. Magnetic measurements showed predominantly paramagnetic behavior for 3ph-imi[FeCl4]. Assembly-1 exhibited weak magnetic hysteresis at 5 K and zero-field-cooled/field-cooled (ZFC–FC) bifurcation below ca. 42 K. In contrast, Assembly-2 showed ZFC–FC bifurcation below ca. 258 K and retained a distinct hysteresis loop at 300 K. The compact molecular packing of the assembled samples may strengthen interactions among neighboring [FeCl4]− units, while the higher structural order and greater spatial continuity of Assembly-2 may support magnetic correlations across larger regions and over a wider temperature range. These findings demonstrate that temperature-regulated aqueous self-assembly provides an effective strategy for tuning the solid-state magnetic properties of small-molecule MILs.

title: Physicochemical Prioritization of Hypothetical Metal–Organic Frameworks for Experimental Synthesis
abstract: The rapid expansion of AI-driven and computationally designed metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) raises a fundamental question: which hypothetical structures are most likely to be experimentally realized? Here, we develop a physicochemically informed strategy to prioritize MOFs for synthesis by integrating molecular synthetic accessibility, framework geometry, electronic structure, solvent removal stability, and thermodynamic stability through positive–unlabeled learning. Using 9,033 experimentally reported MOFs as examples of realized structures and hypothetical MOFs as candidates with unknown synthesizability, we identify 5 complementary physicochemical descriptors that enable effective prioritization, achieving a source-averaged normalized positive rank of 0.93 by placing experimentally realized MOFs near the top of candidate rankings across held-out database sources. Further analysis reveals that experimentally realized MOFs are enriched at low linker geometric distortion and low energy above the convex hull of competing phases, highlighting complementary geometric and thermodynamic considerations. Moreover, secondary building unit–linker analyses identify specific chemical combinations enriched among highly ranked hypothetical structures. Together, these findings establish a chemically interpretable approach to prioritizing hypothetical MOFs and help bridge the gap between computational materials design and experimental synthesis.

title: Dynamic Non‐Covalent Interactions at Oxide–Organic Heterointerfaces Enable Simultaneous Dielectric Enhancement and Mechanical Reinforcement of Organic Photovoltaic Devices and Modules
abstract: ABSTRACT Flexible organic photovoltaics (OPVs) demand both high efficiency and mechanical robustness, yet rigid non‐fullerene acceptor blends commonly suffer from an efficiency–mechanics trade‐off. Here, trace Al 2 O 3 nanofillers are incorporated into the PM6:BTP‐eC9 active layer to simultaneously enhance dielectric screening, charge‐transport balance, and mechanical energy dissipation. The nanofillers raise the relative permittivity from 2.48 to 2.78, promote exciton dissociation, suppress bimolecular and trap‐assisted recombination, and improve charge‐transport balance, raising the power conversion efficiency (PCE) from 16.1% to 17.0% for flexible devices, while increasing that of the corresponding rigid devices from 19.4% to 20.3%. Variable‐temperature FT‐IR spectroscopy and multiscale simulations provide evidence for thermally responsive and partially reversible interactions between Al 2 O 3 surface hydroxyls and polar moieties in the photoactive matrix, which are consistent with hydrogen bonding. These interactions are proposed to enhance intermolecular cohesion, homogenize stress distribution, and suppress crack initiation and propagation, increasing the crack‐onset strain (COS) from 4.6% to 12.0% and nearly quadrupling toughness. The strategy translates to flexible devices retaining 87.3% of their initial efficiency after 2000 bending cycles, intrinsically stretchable devices retaining 79.0% after 200 cycles at 5% strain, and an 11.4%‐efficient flexible module with a 100 cm 2 footprint and 68 cm 2 effective active area.

title: Machine Learning-Driven Electrolyte Additive Discovery for Ultrafast Charging of Sodium Metal Batteries
abstract: Abstract Sodium metal batteries hold immense promise for large-scale, high-power storage systems, yet their fast charging is severely constrained by sluggish Na+ transport across unstable electrode–electrolyte interphases. Conventional fluorine-donating additives suffer from inefficient self-decomposition, inevitably generating resistive organic byproducts. Herein, we propose an active machine learning framework based on Gaussian process regression to develop an innovative additive-triggered anion decomposition pathway. Guided by iterative screening of key physicochemical descriptors, a trace-level (0.02 M) sodium chlorodifluoroacetate (NaCDFA) additive is successfully identified. Theoretical calculations combined with in situ characterizations reveal that the NaCDFA thermodynamically promotes the targeted and continuous decomposition of the PF6– anion, enabling the construction of robust and highly conductive NaF-rich interphases, which substantially reduces the Na+ migration barrier. Consequently, the Na||Na3V2(PO4)3 cell achieves ultrastable cycling over 50,000 cycles at an extreme rate of 200 C. Furthermore, outstanding performance is retained under rigorous practical conditions, including high-mass-loading cathodes and limited sodium excess or anode-free architectures. This work establishes a cost-effective trace-level electrolyte additive strategy for engineering fast-charging interphases, and demonstrates the transformative potential of machine learning-guided materials discovery for advancing battery technology.

title: Closed- vs Open-Shell: Unlocking Doublet Emission in Persistent Phosphorus-Containing Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon Radicals
abstract: Abstract Persistent organic radicals embedded in conjugated materials are extremely rare due to the scarcity of suitable structural motifs capable of stabilizing unpaired spins. Here, we present a phosphorus-incorporated polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon scaffold, along with its respective chemically reduced open-shell relatives, that provides access to these radical species. Two strategically placed keto groups activate new conjugation pathways that, coupled with two phosphoryl moieties, gives rise to a strongly electron-accepting molecular architecture. The resulting radical species demonstrate persistence in THF up to a week and are remarkably stable in ethanol, a feature rarely observed for π-system radicals. Despite the presence of the keto groups in the framework, the P-based closed-shell compounds display intense fluorescence with quantum yields of up to 54%. More importantly, the corresponding radicals are also emissive, constituting the first isolated luminescent radicals in conjugated organophosphorus materials. Intriguingly, these species feature dual doublet emission at room temperature that occurs through two distinct radiative pathways: one following Kasha’s rule and the other constituting a rare anti-Kasha process.

title: Mg(II)/H-Bonding Catalyst Design for Asymmetric Amination–Protonation Reaction
abstract: Abstract Given the strong interaction between amine and ketone groups, which often act as catalyst–substrate partners via iminium ion catalysis, the catalytic asymmetric aza-conjugate addition of common cyclic amines to unsaturated enones has never been successfully achieved. This model reaction is inherently challenging due to both the self-racemization of the amino–ketone products and the autocatalysis arising from the amine–ketone interaction. Consequently, this most straightforward and efficient route to chiral γ-amino alcohols remains unrealized to date. Herein, through the rational design of a novel Mg(II)/H-bonding catalytic strategy based on newly developed trihydroxyl chiral ligands, we have successfully suppressed the self-activation pathway between amines and conjugated enones, thereby achieving the desired amination–protonation reaction with high enantioselectivities. This new catalytic system proves highly effective for the one-pot synthesis of diverse chiral γ-amino alcohols bearing tertiary or quaternary stereocenters. Mechanistic investigations, including the identification of the formed metal complex and the true catalytically active species, the study of key transition states, and the elucidation of the coordination details of the Mg(II)/H-bonding catalyst through DFT-optimized processes, support a plausible mechanism for the asymmetric amination–protonation process.

title: Ferroionic‐Assisted, Charge‐Driven Polymorphic Phase Engineering for Multilevel Memristive Devices
abstract: ABSTRACT Memristive device operation can arise from diverse microscopic mechanisms, including charge polarization and trapping, magnetic ordering, ionic migration, and structural phase transitions. Among these, crystalline–crystalline phase transitions in polymorphic materials offer a unique platform for nonvolatile resistance modulation but are often hindered by large energy barriers and limited endurance. Here, we demonstrate a multimodal, charge‐driven phase modulation in an atomically thin polymorphic material, Mo 0.92 W 0.08 Te 2 , enabled by electrostatic coupling to a ferroionic substrate, CuInP 2 S 6 . The polymorphic channel exhibits reversible switching between semiconducting and metallic phases via electrostatically accumulated charges, reflecting the intrinsically low energy barrier between its competing polymorphs. Integration with the ferroionic substrate enables spatially localized, nonvolatile charge accumulation in the channel, which provides distinct, programmable phase‐control pathways under a two‐terminal bias configuration. The phase‐induced resistance modulation through field‐driven ionic processes is governed by the evolution of a phase‐dependent Schottky junction at the electrode–channel interface, yielding multiple, stable conductance states under pulsed electrical excitation. Leveraging these experimentally derived synaptic characteristics, we conducted an MNIST inference simulation with a convolutional neural network, achieving 98.45% accuracy. This ferroionic‐assisted phase‐engineering strategy offers new opportunities beyond traditional phase‐change devices for adaptive electronic and neuromorphic material platforms.

title: Mechanically Tunable Quantum Transport in Graphene Nanoribbons with Antiaromatic Motifs
abstract: Abstract Nonbenzenoid graphene nanoribbons provide a versatile platform for tailoring electronic structures beyond conventional benzenoid π-conjugated systems, yet the impact of their topology on quantum transport remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate electrical conductance through suspended ladder phenylene nanoribbons containing antiaromatic four-membered rings using scanning tunneling microscope lifting spectroscopy. As the nanoribbon is progressively detached from the substrate, differential conductance measurements reveal successive charge-state transitions accompanied by alternating Kondo resonances, demonstrating the dynamic generation of localized spins in an intrinsically closed-shell nanoribbon. Density functional theory calculations show that the antiaromatic topology reduces the HOMO–LUMO gap and induces a pronounced length dependence of the occupied frontier orbitals, which shift progressively toward and eventually across the electrode Fermi level with increasing suspended length, driving successive charge-state transitions. The transport behavior is quantitatively described within a double-barrier tunneling framework incorporating charge quantization and many-body interactions. These results suggest an antiaromaticity-driven mechanism for charge-state evolution and propose antiaromaticity as a molecular design principle for controlling charge and spin states in nonbenzenoid carbon nanostructures.

title: Ambipolar Fiber Amplifiers for Highly Sensitive Biosignal Detection
abstract: ABSTRACT Biological signals are inherently weak and susceptible to noise, making in situ signal amplification critical for high‐fidelity sensing. Electronic fibers offer unique advantages for conformal and scalable biointegration; however, fiber amplifiers are seldom reported due to the lack of suitable semiconducting materials that combine balanced ambipolar transport, scalable fiber fabrication, and high device performance. Herein, we report the first single‐component ambipolar fiber platform based on a newly designed polymer, P(gTDPP‐TQ), which combines balanced p‐ and n‐type transport, low‐cost synthesis, and continuous fiber fabrication. Fiber processing enhances molecular ordering and charge transport, yielding record‐high µC * and g m,norm among reported semiconducting fibers, enabling high‐performance fiber amplifiers with a high voltage gain of up to 150 V V −1 and low operating voltages down to 0.5 V. These fiber amplifiers enable high‐fidelity electroencephalogram signal amplification over 20 times and sensitive cortisol sensing with a record‐low detection limit of 3.7 fM. This work establishes a general ambipolar fiber platform for integrated bioelectronic amplification and sensing.

title: Heterostructure Design in Two‐Dimensional Perovskites by Sequential Recrystallization
abstract: ABSTRACT Low‐dimensional metal halide perovskites provide exciting opportunities to fabricate new semiconductor materials. Semiconductor technology relies on electronic heterojunctions, and cost‐efficient and flexible approaches to realize functional heterostructures are of fundamental importance. Lateral heterostructures define the energy landscape in the plane of the semiconducting lattice in 2D perovskite materials, representing an ideal platform to tailor energy barriers and to control charge carrier flow. Here, we demonstrate a versatile one‐pot synthesis to fabricate a large variety of 2D perovskite heterostructures based on different halides and/or metal cations. Exploiting sequential crystallization of different 2D perovskites and tuning the composition and injection events of the materials, enables the design of diverse heterostructure architectures, including multiple heterojunctions. We obtain heterostructures with high crystalline quality, multicolor emission, and optical coupling between the different heterostructure regions. We foresee that the design freedom of our method will stimulate the development of novel optoelectronic devices where electronic band engineering is crucial.

title: Porphyrin Integration Enhances Bipolar Redox Accessibility for High‐Rate Sodium‐Based Dual‐Ion Storage
abstract: ABSTRACT Closing the gap between theoretical multielectron capacity and practical accessibility remains the central bottleneck for high‐energy organic batteries. Herein, we report a molecular design strategy that integrates a porphyrin motif into a sulfur‐rich conjugated polymer (BTTP) to align electronic structure, state‐dependent ion interactions, and electrochemical kinetics across the bipolar window. Despite possessing a lower theoretical capacity than its reference counterpart (BTB), BTTP achieves an exceptional theoretical capacity utilization of 94.2% (delivering 477 mAh g −1 at 0.5 A g −1 , compared to only 53.5% and 351 mAh g −1 for BTB). Electrokinetic analyses, including GITT and DRT, confirm accelerated apparent ion diffusion and reduced polarization limitations, enabling BTTP to retain 166 mAh g −1 at an ultrahigh current density of 20 A g −1 over 25 000 cycles. Operando/ex situ spectroscopy and theoretical calculations elucidate that the dual pyrrolic/imino nitrogen sites in porphyrin and the sulfur‐rich backbone cooperatively provide potential‐dependent coordination environments for PF 6 − anions and Na + cations. This work suggests that molecular regulation of complementary ion‐interaction environments within multi‐active‐unit frameworks, rather than simply increasing the number of redox units, is important for enhancing rate capability and capacity utilization.

title: Palladium‐Catalyzed Synthesis of Multisubstituted Conjugated Dienes from Unactivated Alkenes
abstract: ABSTRACT The efficient and stereoselective synthesis of multisubstituted conjugated 1,3‐dienes remains a longstanding challenge because of the difficulty in controlling regioselectivity and stereochemistry. In this study, we report a ligand‐promoted, carboxylate‐directed palladium‐catalyzed alkenylation of unactivated alkenes with vinyl iodides for the modular synthesis of multisubstituted conjugated 1,3‐dienes. A bulky norbornane‐based monophosphine ligand (NBphos) is key to overcoming the intrinsically low reactivity and poor regiocontrol of unactivated alkenes, enabling efficient coupling with high regio‐ and stereoselectivity. The protocol provides access to a broad range of multisubstituted 1,3‐dienes, including highly congested pentasubstituted derivatives. Notably, stereodivergent synthesis of either diene stereoisomer is achieved directly from the corresponding E ‐ or Z ‐configured alkene substrates. The synthetic utility of the method is demonstrated through the derivatization of glycals and diverse downstream Diels–Alder transformations. Mechanistic studies reveal that a free carboxylic acid is indispensable for directing the palladium‐catalyzed alkenylation, underscoring the critical role of substrate coordination in achieving the observed reactivity and selectivity.

title: Carbon Nanofiber-Integrated CuCo-MOF as a Conductive Bifunctional Electrocatalyst for Overall Water Splitting
abstract: Abstract The CuCo-MOF/CNF electrocatalyst, with a well-defined microstructure and efficient charge transfer was successfully synthesized through a simple solvothermal method. In the CuCo-MOF/CNF composite, the introduction of CNF can effectively improve the conductivity and provide sufficient active sites for the electrochemical reaction. The CuCo-MOF/CNF composite has excellent bifunctional electrocatalytic activity for the HER and OER reactions. The catalyst really stands out with its great performance, requiring overpotentials of 50 mV for HER and 70 mV for OER at a current density of 10 mA cm–2. The CuCo-MOF/CNF electrocatalyst has low Tafel slope values of 98 mV dec–1 for OER and 131 mV dec–1 for HER, along with low charge transfer resistance, exhibiting excellent operational stability for up to 40 h for both OER and HER. Moreover, the catalyst has relatively large double-layer capacitance values of 8.95 mF cm–2 for OER and 3.47 mF cm–2 for HER, implying that the electrochemically active surface areas are quite large (223.8 cm2 for OER and 86.8 cm2 for HER). Overall, these structural and electrochemical advantages contribute to the superior catalytic performance of the electrocatalyst, providing a novel framework for the development of highly efficient and scalable bifunctional electrocatalysts for overall water splitting.

title: In vitro–reconstituted Drosophila Arc capsids deliver gene editors to dystrophic muscle
abstract: Abstract The intracellular delivery of therapeutic macromolecules remains a major challenge in biomedicine. Capsid-forming proteins are one promising vehicle, but to date, these have required cellular assembly or rely on fusogens for cell entry, limiting their scalability and utility. Here we reconstitute the Drosophila melanogaster Arc1 (dArc1) retroelement-derived capsid entirely from purified recombinant protein components and in vitro transcribed RNA, creating a fully defined, cell-free assembled protein nanoparticle system. We engineered the dArc1 RNA-binding domain to efficiently encapsulate both mRNA payloads and Cas9 ribonucleoproteins. We show that dArc1 capsids bind mammalian cells through a direct interaction with the surface receptor SORCS2. Leveraging this interaction, we demonstrate that intramuscular injection of dArc1 capsids carrying Cas9 gene editors achieves up to 18% exon skipping and restores dystrophin expression in muscle fibers of mdx mice, a model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy. This work demonstrates the potential of in vitro-assembled protein nanoparticles for delivery of molecular cargoes.
